title: Nicklaus Concedes the Putt to Jacklin
text:
In September 1969 the Ryder Cup between the United States and Great Britain was played at Royal Birkdale in England. It was one of the closest contests in the event's history. On the last afternoon everything came down to the final singles match, between Jack Nicklaus of the United States and Tony Jacklin of Britain, who had just won the Open Championship and was a national hero.

They came to the 18th hole all square. Both reached the green. Nicklaus holed his putt for par, leaving Jacklin a short putt of about two feet to halve the hole, the match and the whole Ryder Cup. If he missed, the Americans would win outright.

Nicklaus did not make him putt it. He picked up Jacklin's marker, conceding the putt. By most accounts he told Jacklin he did not think he would have missed, but he was not going to give him the chance in those circumstances.

The match was halved and the Ryder Cup tied at 16 points each. The Americans kept the trophy as holders, but some of Nicklaus's teammates and his captain were unhappy. The gesture became known simply as "the Concession" and is remembered as one of the great acts of sportsmanship in golf.
lesson: Sometimes how a contest ends matters more than who edges ahead. A generous gesture at the decisive moment is remembered long after the score is forgotten.
location: Royal Birkdale Golf Club, Southport, England
source: Contemporary press reports of the 1969 Ryder Cup; Jack Nicklaus, My Story (1997)
